design: Each session takes about 20 minutes: learn (5 min), try (10 min), reflect (5 min). Baseline areas get 1 session; deep areas get 3. Goals are written as observable behaviour (action mapping). {{task}} is replaced with the learner's own work task. Practice always uses made-up details.

understand.goal: I can explain what AI is good at, where it goes wrong, and when not to use it.
understand.check: I can name one task AI helps me with and one it shouldn't do.

sessions.title: What AI is, and what it isn't
sessions.learn: AI tools predict likely words or images from patterns in their training. They can sound confident and still be wrong.
sessions.learn_ca: AI tools predict likely words or images from patterns in their training. They can sound confident and still be wrong. The free national course, AI for All: Essentials for Canadians, covers this well if you want more.
sessions.try: Ask an approved AI tool a question about your field that you already know the answer to. Note one thing it got right and one thing it got wrong or left vague.
sessions.reflect: Where in my work would a confident but wrong answer cause the most trouble?

sessions.title: Why AI gets things wrong
sessions.learn: Common failures: made-up facts and sources, outdated information, bias picked up from training data, and answers that sound more certain than they should.
sessions.try: Ask the same question three different ways. Compare the answers and note where they disagree.
sessions.reflect: Which of these failures would be hardest for me to notice?

sessions.title: Knowing when not to use AI
sessions.learn: Some work should stay with people: decisions about people, anything confidential, and work where someone must be accountable for every word.
sessions.try: List three tasks in your work where you would not use AI, and write one sentence on why for each.
sessions.try_executives: Bring one 'what could go wrong' scenario to your next leadership meeting, and agree on a guardrail for it.
sessions.reflect: What would I say to a colleague who asked me when AI isn't the right tool?

explore.goal: I can find tasks in my work where AI helps, and tasks where it doesn't.
explore.check: I have tried AI on one real task and decided whether to keep using it there.

sessions.title: Spot the opportunities
sessions.learn: AI tends to help most with drafting, summarizing, sorting, brainstorming and reformatting. It helps least where accuracy, judgment or relationships matter most.
sessions.try: List the tasks you do in a typical week. Mark each one: could AI help, maybe, or no.
sessions.reflect: Which task would save me the most time or stress if AI helped?

sessions.title: Try one task from start to finish
sessions.learn: A small, real trial teaches more than a demo. Pick one task, use an approved tool, and judge the result honestly.
sessions.try: Use an approved tool on this task: {{task}}. Use made-up details in place of anything real or confidential.
sessions.reflect: Was the result faster, better, or neither? What would I change next time?

sessions.title: Share what you found
sessions.learn: Wins and failures are both useful. Sharing them helps your team learn faster and keeps examples real.
sessions.try: Share one thing that worked and one that didn't with a colleague or your team.
sessions.try_executives: With your leadership team, pick two uses of AI worth trying, and agree on what guardrails each one needs.
sessions.reflect: What did I learn from someone else's example?

direct.goal: I can give an AI tool clear instructions and context to get a useful result.
direct.check: I get a usable first draft within three tries.

sessions.title: Give clear instructions
sessions.learn: Good instructions cover five things: who the AI should act as, the task, the context, the format you want, and an example if you have one.
sessions.try: Write a vague request for this task: {{task}}. Then rewrite it using all five parts, with made-up details. Compare the two results.
sessions.reflect: Which of the five parts made the biggest difference?

sessions.title: Improve the answer, don't settle
sessions.learn: The first answer is a starting point. Follow-up requests like 'shorter', 'for a new employee' or 'what's missing?' often matter more than the first one.
sessions.try: Take one result and improve it with three follow-up requests. Keep notes on what each one changed.
sessions.reflect: When should I stop refining and do it myself?

sessions.title: Build a reusable prompt
sessions.learn: If you do a task often, a saved set of instructions makes results more consistent and easier to check.
sessions.try: Write a reusable set of instructions for this task: {{task}}. Save it, and share it with a colleague to try.
sessions.reflect: What would make this easy for someone else on my team to use?

evaluate.goal: I check AI output before I use it, especially facts, figures, names and links.
evaluate.check: I found and fixed at least one error in AI output this month.

sessions.title: Check before you trust
sessions.learn: Check the things AI most often gets wrong: facts, figures, names, quotes, dates and links. If it matters, confirm it in the original source.
sessions.try: Ask an AI tool to summarize a public document you know well. Find anything it got wrong, left out or added.

sessions.title: Spot made-up details
sessions.learn: AI can invent sources, statistics and quotes that look real. A citation is not proof until you have opened it.
sessions.try: Ask an AI tool for three statistics about your field, with sources. Check each one.
sessions.reflect: How many held up? How will that change how I use AI answers?

sessions.title: Make checking a habit
sessions.learn: A short personal checklist turns checking into a habit instead of a chore.
sessions.try: Write a three-to-five item checklist for AI output in your work. Use it on your next real AI-assisted task.
sessions.try_managers: With your team, agree on what 'checked' means before AI-assisted work is shared, and write it down.
sessions.reflect: What will remind me to use the checklist when I'm busy?

responsible.goal: I know what never goes into an AI tool, and I use approved tools.
responsible.check: I can find our AI policy and approved-tools list, and I haven't entered anything on the never list.

sessions.title: The data red lines
sessions.learn: Never enter personal information about others, passwords or credentials, unreleased financials, trade secrets, or anything under a confidentiality agreement.
sessions.learn_ca: Never enter personal information about others, passwords or credentials, unreleased financials, trade secrets, or anything under a confidentiality agreement. In Canada, privacy laws such as PIPEDA and provincial laws apply to personal information, including what goes into AI tools.
sessions.try: Find your organization's AI policy and approved-tools list. Then sort six everyday items from your work into 'fine to use' and 'never'.
sessions.reflect: Which item was hardest to decide, and who could I ask?

sessions.title: Safe ways to get the help
sessions.learn: You can often get the same help without the risky details: remove names, use placeholders, or describe the situation in general terms.
sessions.try: Take this task: {{task}}. Rewrite what you would give the AI so that it contains nothing on the never list.
sessions.reflect: Did removing the details change the quality of the help?

sessions.title: Being open about AI use
sessions.learn: Being open about when AI helped builds trust, and lets others check the work properly.
sessions.try: Decide when you'll tell others that AI helped with your work, and write it as a personal rule.
sessions.try_managers: Run a 15-minute team huddle to agree on three team rules for AI use. Write them down where everyone can see them.
sessions.reflect: What would make it easy for people on my team to be open about AI use?

build.label: Build with AI (beyond the framework)
build.goal: I can build AI into tools and workflows with human review, testing and logging.
build.check: Every AI feature I build has a named reviewer, test cases and a log.

sessions.title: Design for human review
sessions.learn: Decide where a person checks AI output, and what happens when confidence is low or the stakes are high.
sessions.try: Sketch one AI workflow you could build, and mark exactly where a person reviews the output.
sessions.reflect: What would happen if nobody did the review?

sessions.title: Test before you trust
sessions.learn: AI features need test cases like any other code, including edge cases and inputs that should be refused.
sessions.try: Write five test cases for your workflow, including two edge cases and one input it should refuse.
sessions.reflect: Which test am I least sure it would pass?

sessions.title: Log and govern
sessions.learn: Light logging of inputs, outputs and errors makes AI work auditable. The NIST AI Risk Management Framework is a practical guide.
sessions.try: Decide what your workflow should log, who reviews a sample each month, and who owns it.
sessions.reflect: Who would I call if this workflow went wrong at 2 a.m.?

self_assessment.understand: I can explain in my own words what AI tools are good at, and where they go wrong.
self_assessment.explore: I can spot tasks in my own work where AI could help.
self_assessment.direct: I can give an AI tool clear instructions and context to get a useful result.
self_assessment.evaluate: I could spot a factual error in an AI-generated draft.
self_assessment.responsible: I know which information should never go into an AI tool.
self_assessment.build: I can build AI into a tool or workflow safely.
